categories.name: Structure & organization
categories.q: Are the expected parts there, in a sensible order, with sound proportions?

categories.name: Clarity & readability
categories.q: Can the intended reader follow the prose without strain?

categories.name: Style & concision
categories.q: Is the writing direct, economical and free of filler?

categories.name: Mechanics & spelling
categories.q: Is the text free of typos, doubled words and punctuation slips?

categories.name: Grammar & usage
categories.q: Are the sentences grammatical and the words the right ones?

categories.name: Flow & cohesion
categories.q: Does each paragraph and sentence follow from the one before?

categories.name: Evidence & citations
categories.q: Are claims supported, and do citations and references line up?

categories.name: Consistency & terminology
categories.q: Are terms, spellings, numbers and cross-references handled the same way throughout?

categories.name: Completeness & integrity
categories.q: Is this a finished manuscript, with no placeholders, stubs, duplicates or open edits?

rules.name: Required sections
rules.desc: Share of the sections this document type is expected to have that were found as headings or labelled paragraphs.
rules.why: Journals and publishers expect a recognisable skeleton (IMRaD for research papers). Readers and reviewers navigate by it.
rules.fix: Add the missing sections, or rename existing headings so their role is clear.

critical.label: Missing any of these is critical

ex: Sections: Introduction, Our Work, Final Thoughts
Sections: Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, References

rules.name: Section order
rules.desc: Expected sections that appear out of the conventional order (Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Conclusion, References).
rules.why: The conventional order lets readers find methods before results and conclusions after evidence.
rules.fix: Move the flagged sections into the conventional order, or explain the deviation.

rules.name: Heading hierarchy
rules.desc: Headings that skip a level (a level-1 heading followed directly by level 3), and long documents with no headings at all.
rules.why: A skipped level breaks the outline, the table of contents, and screen-reader navigation.
rules.fix: Insert the missing intermediate heading or promote the deeper one.

min_words_for_headings.label: Expect headings above this many words

rules.name: Paragraph length
rules.desc: Share of paragraphs longer than the word limit.
rules.why: Very long paragraphs hide the topic sentence and tire the reader; most style guides advise one idea per paragraph.
rules.fix: Split each long paragraph at its natural turns of thought.
ex: One 320-word paragraph covering the sample, the instrument and the analysis.
Three paragraphs: sample (90 words), instrument (110), analysis (120).

rules.name: One-sentence paragraphs
rules.desc: Share of paragraphs made of a single sentence (paragraphs under 8 words are ignored).
rules.why: In expository writing a single-sentence paragraph usually means an undeveloped point or a fragment of a neighbour.
rules.fix: Develop the point with evidence or merge it into the adjacent paragraph.
ex: Sleep matters because it stabilises new memories; even short naps help (Lahl et al., 2008).

rules.name: Section balance
rules.desc: Coefficient of variation of the word counts of top-level sections (3 or more sections needed).
rules.why: Wildly uneven sections or chapters usually signal a missing split or an under-developed part.
rules.fix: Split oversized sections; expand or merge undersized ones.
ex: Chapter 1: 800 words · Chapter 2: 9,400 words · Chapter 3: 1,100 words

rules.name: Abstract length
rules.desc: Word count of the abstract.
rules.why: Most journals cap abstracts at 150-300 words; indexing services truncate longer ones.
rules.fix: Trim to the journal limit: problem, method, key result, implication.
ex: A 480-word abstract that retells the introduction.
A 220-word abstract: problem, method, key result with numbers, implication.

rules.name: Document length
rules.desc: Total words of body text (references and tables excluded).
rules.why: Venues and publishers set length expectations; far outside them a submission is returned unread.
rules.fix: Cut or expand to the venue's range.
ex: A 1,200-word submission to a journal that asks for 4,000–8,000.

rules.name: Title
rules.desc: Title present, within the word limit, not in all capitals, no full stop, no unexplained abbreviations.
rules.why: The title is what indexes, search engines and editors read first.
rules.fix: Write a specific, concise title without abbreviations or a full stop.
ex: A STUDY OF THE EFFECTS OF NAPS ON MEM.
Short Daytime Naps Improve Word-Pair Recall in Students

rules.name: Aim or research question stated
rules.desc: Whether the introduction says what the work sets out to do ('this paper examines', 'we test whether', 'our research question').
rules.why: Reviewers judge everything else against the stated aim; a missing aim is a standard major comment.
rules.fix: State the aim, question or hypothesis explicitly near the end of the introduction.
ex: Sleep is important. Many people nap. Memory is complex.
This study tests whether a 20-minute nap improves recall of word pairs.

rules.name: Lone subsections
rules.desc: Sections that contain exactly one subsection (a 2.1 with no 2.2).
rules.why: Dividing a section into one part is not a division; outline conventions require two or more.
rules.fix: Add a second subsection or remove the lone subheading.

rules.name: Long headings
rules.desc: Headings longer than the word limit.
rules.why: Headings are signposts; long ones stop being scannable.
rules.fix: Cut the heading to its key phrase.
ex: 2.3 How We Recruited, Screened, Consented and Scheduled the Participants for Sessions

rules.name: Introduction share
rules.desc: The introduction's share of the body text.
rules.why: An introduction that takes over the paper squeezes methods and results; one that is too thin fails to motivate.
rules.fix: Rebalance: trim background or expand the motivation.
ex: Introduction ≈ 15% of the paper, Methods and Results carry the weight.

rules.name: Abstract content
rules.desc: Abstract cites references, reports no concrete result (no numbers), or runs to several paragraphs.
rules.why: Most journals require a single-paragraph abstract with key results and no citations.
rules.fix: Remove citations, add the main quantitative finding, merge into one paragraph.
ex: Abstract: Prior work [3, 7] shows… We discuss implications.

rules.name: Keyword count
rules.desc: Number of keywords listed.
rules.why: Journals usually ask for 3 to 8 keywords for indexing.
rules.fix: List 3 to 8 specific keywords not already in the title.
ex: Keywords: daytime napping; declarative memory; consolidation; word-pair recall

rules.name: New material in the conclusion
rules.desc: Citations and figure or table references inside the conclusion.
rules.why: A conclusion should draw together what was shown, not introduce new evidence.
rules.fix: Move new citations or figures into the discussion.
ex: Conclusion: Short naps improved recall; schedule them between study and test.

rules.name: Heading numbering
rules.desc: Mixed numbered and unnumbered headings, and numbering that skips or repeats (1, 2, 4 or 2.1, 2.3).
rules.why: Broken numbering usually means a section was deleted or moved without renumbering.
rules.fix: Renumber the headings in sequence and number all or none.

rules.name: Chapter length
rules.desc: Share of chapters (top-level sections) whose length falls outside the target range.
rules.why: Readers and publishers expect roughly even chapter lengths for pacing.
rules.fix: Split long chapters, merge or expand short ones.

rules.name: Reading grade
rules.desc: Flesch-Kincaid grade level of the body text.
rules.why: The grade should match the audience: about 12-16 for scholarly work, 7-10 for general non-fiction.
rules.fix: Shorten sentences and prefer common words to lower it; the opposite raises it.
ex: Grade 22: dense clauses of polysyllabic abstractions throughout.
Grade 14: technical terms kept, sentences shortened.

rules.name: Long sentences
rules.desc: Share of sentences longer than the word limit.
rules.why: Comprehension drops sharply beyond about 25-30 words per sentence.
rules.fix: Split at conjunctions and semicolons; move qualifications into their own sentence.
ex: We recruited students who, because they had classes in the afternoon and often drank coffee, were likely to nap poorly, which we expected to reduce the effect.
We recruited students with afternoon classes. Many drank coffee, which we expected to weaken the nap effect.

rules.name: Very long sentences
rules.desc: Sentences over the hard limit, counted per 1,000 words.
rules.why: Sentences this long are almost always two or three sentences fused together.
rules.fix: Break each flagged sentence into two or more.
ex: A 64-word sentence with three clauses joined by 'and', 'which' and 'because'.

rules.name: Passive voice
rules.desc: Share of sentences containing a passive construction (form of 'to be' + past participle).
rules.why: Passive voice hides who did what. Some is normal in methods sections; heavy use slows every reader.
rules.fix: Name the actor: 'we measured' instead of 'it was measured'.
ex: The samples were analysed and the results were recorded.
We analysed the samples and recorded the results.

rules.name: Sentence variety
rules.desc: Standard deviation of sentence length in words.
rules.why: Uniform sentence length produces monotonous prose; varied length keeps attention.
rules.fix: Mix short emphatic sentences with longer explanatory ones.
ex: Twelve sentences in a row of 18–21 words.
Mix: a 6-word claim, a 25-word explanation, a 14-word example.

rules.name: Complex words
rules.desc: Share of words with three or more syllables (not counting -ed, -es, -ing endings).
rules.why: Polysyllabic density is the main driver of reading difficulty (Gunning fog index).
rules.fix: Prefer the shorter common word where it says the same thing.
ex: The operationalization of multidimensional organizational variables…
We measured three aspects of how the company is organized…

rules.name: Preposition chains
rules.desc: Sentences with four or more uses of 'of'.
rules.why: Chains like 'the analysis of the effect of the size of the sample' bury the subject.
rules.fix: Use possessives, compound nouns or a verb to break the chain.
ex: the analysis of the effect of the size of the sample of the study

rules.name: Parenthetical overload
rules.desc: Sentences with three or more parenthetical asides, or nested brackets.
rules.why: Every parenthesis interrupts the main line of thought.
rules.fix: Promote important asides to their own sentence, drop the rest.
ex: Naps (short ones (under 30 min)) help (see Table 2) students (mostly).
Short naps (under 30 minutes) help most students (Table 2).

rules.name: Number-dense sentences
rules.desc: Sentences containing six or more numbers.
rules.why: Readers can't hold that many values in their head; a table does it better.
rules.fix: Move the numbers into a table and state the pattern in words.
ex: Scores ranged from 26.9 to 31.2 across the six days (Table 3).

rules.name: Vague 'this' openers
rules.desc: Sentences that start with This, That, These or Those followed directly by a verb ('This shows…').
rules.why: A bare 'this' forces the reader to guess what it refers to.
rules.fix: Add the noun: 'This result shows…'.
ex: This 14% improvement shows the method works.

rules.name: Nominalizations
rules.desc: Verbs turned into nouns (-tion, -ment, -ance, -ence, -ity, -ness).
rules.why: 'Make an assessment of' hides the action that 'assess' states directly (Williams, Style).
rules.fix: Turn the noun back into a verb.
ex: We made an assessment of the implementation of the intervention.
We assessed how the intervention was implemented.

rules.name: Front-loaded sentences
rules.desc: Sentences that open with a subordinate clause of more than 15 words before the main clause.
rules.why: Readers wait for the subject and verb; a long wind-up taxes working memory.
rules.fix: Put the main clause first or split the sentence.
ex: Although prior studies conducted in laboratory settings with long naps and strict schedules reported benefits, we…
We tested short naps in real student schedules, unlike prior laboratory studies of long naps.

rules.name: Wordy phrases
rules.desc: Phrases with a shorter equivalent ('in order to' -> 'to', 'due to the fact that' -> 'because').
rules.why: Every style guide from Strunk & White to the APA manual asks for the shortest clear wording.
rules.fix: Replace each phrase with the suggested short form.
ex: In order to test this, due to the fact that…

rules.name: Hedges & intensifiers
rules.desc: Words such as very, really, quite, clearly, obviously, basically, somewhat.
rules.why: Intensifiers weaken the claims they decorate, and 'clearly' or 'obviously' annoy reviewers when the point is not obvious.
rules.fix: Delete the word, or replace it with a precise quantity or a citation.
ex: This is a very really important and clearly novel result.
This result is new and doubles recall.

rules.name: Clichés & stock phrases
rules.desc: Worn phrases ('at the end of the day', 'paradigm shift', 'plays a crucial role', 'in today's world').
rules.why: Stock phrases signal autopilot writing and carry little information.
rules.fix: Say the specific thing the phrase stands in for.
ex: At the end of the day, napping plays a crucial role.

rules.name: Repeated sentence openings
rules.desc: Runs of three or more consecutive sentences in a paragraph starting with the same word.
rules.why: Repeated openings create a list-like drone and hide the logical links between sentences.
rules.fix: Vary the openings or combine the sentences.
ex: We measured… We tested… We found… We concluded…
We measured… Testing showed… These findings suggest…

rules.name: Word echoes
rules.desc: The same content word used three or more times in one sentence, or twice for a rare word.
rules.why: Close repetition reads as careless unless it is deliberate emphasis.
rules.fix: Use a pronoun, a synonym, or restructure the sentence.
ex: The laboratory naps in the laboratory differ from laboratory conditions.
Naps in the laboratory differ from those at home.

rules.name: Adverb density
rules.desc: Share of words that are -ly adverbs.
rules.why: Heavy adverb use usually props up weak verbs.
rules.fix: Choose a stronger verb and drop the adverb.
ex: She quickly and quietly carefully opened the door.

rules.name: First-person singular
rules.desc: Uses of I, me, my, mine, myself.
rules.why: Many scholarly venues prefer 'we' or impersonal constructions; check your venue's guide.
rules.fix: Rephrase, or switch this rule off if your venue allows it.

rules.name: Contractions
rules.desc: Contractions such as don't, can't, it's, we're.
rules.why: Formal academic registers avoid contractions.
rules.fix: Expand each contraction.
ex: We didn't find effects that weren't expected.
We did not find unexpected effects.

rules.name: Exclamation marks
rules.desc: Exclamation marks in body text.
rules.why: Formal writing earns emphasis through content, not punctuation.
rules.fix: Replace with a full stop.

rules.name: Inclusive language
rules.desc: Terms that style guides (APA 7, Chicago 18) flag as non-inclusive, e.g. mankind, manpower, chairman, he or she.
rules.why: Inclusive wording is now required by most publishers' style guides.
rules.fix: Use the suggested neutral alternative.
ex: the chairman will review manpower needs
the chair will review staffing needs

rules.name: Expletive constructions
rules.desc: Sentences opening with 'There is/are' or 'It is … that/to'.
rules.why: Expletives push the real subject later and add words.
rules.fix: Start with the real subject: 'Many studies exist' → 'Studies …'.
ex: There are many students who nap.

rules.name: Buzzwords & pompous words
rules.desc: Words like utilize, leverage, synergy, holistic, facilitate, aforementioned, herein.
rules.why: Plain-language guidelines (US Plain Writing Act, UK GOV.UK style) ban these as needlessly inflated.
rules.fix: Use the plain alternative shown.

rules.name: Redundant pairs
rules.desc: Pleonasms such as 'past history', 'exact same', 'general consensus', 'period of time', 'still remains'.
rules.why: One of the two words already carries the meaning.
rules.fix: Drop the redundant word.

rules.name: Negative phrasing
rules.desc: Negatives with a direct positive form ('not able' → unable, 'did not remember' → forgot, 'not unlike' → like).
rules.why: Strunk & White: put statements in positive form; double hedges like 'not uncommon' are hard to parse.
rules.fix: Use the positive form.
ex: The data was not uncommon and we did not remember the cause.
The data was common and we forgot the cause.

rules.name: Sentences starting with And / But / So
rules.desc: Sentences beginning with a coordinating conjunction.
rules.why: Acceptable in modern prose but most academic venues still discourage it.
rules.fix: Join to the previous sentence or use However / Therefore.
ex: And the effect held. But only for women.
The effect held, but only for women.

rules.name: Rhetorical questions
rules.desc: Questions in the body text outside quotations.
rules.why: Scholarly writing states claims; rhetorical questions defer them.
rules.fix: Turn the question into the statement you want the reader to accept.
ex: Why does sleep matter? It matters because…

rules.name: Transition overuse
rules.desc: Sentences opening with However, Moreover, Furthermore, Additionally, Thus, Therefore…
rules.why: Stacked transitions read as padding and blunt the ones that matter.
rules.fix: Keep a transition only where the logical link is not already obvious.
ex: Use transitions only where the logical turn isn't obvious.

rules.name: Informal register
rules.desc: Informal words (gonna, kinda, a lot, stuff, huge, awesome, okay).
rules.why: Formal writing keeps a consistent register.
rules.fix: Replace with the formal equivalent.
ex: We got a lot of awesome data.

rules.name: Second person
rules.desc: Uses of you, your, yourself.
rules.why: Most academic styles avoid addressing the reader directly.
rules.fix: Rephrase impersonally or with 'readers' / 'researchers'.
ex: You can see that your results will vary.

rules.name: Repeated paragraph openings
rules.desc: Three or more consecutive paragraphs starting with the same word.
rules.why: Identical openings make paragraphs feel like a list and hide their links.
rules.fix: Vary the openings to signal how each paragraph moves the argument.
ex: The data… Two patterns stand out… Unlike earlier work…

rules.name: Vague words
rules.desc: Low-information words: thing, stuff, aspect, various, nice, interesting, a lot.
rules.why: Vague nouns and adjectives make the reader supply the meaning.
rules.fix: Name the actual thing or quantity.
ex: Various factors and things affect this aspect.
Caffeine, noise and nap length affect recall.

rules.name: Gendered generic pronouns
rules.desc: He / his / him referring back to a generic person ('each participant … his').
rules.why: APA 7 and Chicago 18 recommend singular 'they' or plural forms for generic people.
rules.fix: Use 'they', make the noun plural, or rephrase.

rules.name: Dialogue tags
rules.desc: Showy dialogue tags (exclaimed, retorted, hissed, chuckled) and adverbs after 'said' ('said softly').
rules.why: Editors favour invisible tags ('said', 'asked') and let dialogue carry the emotion.
rules.fix: Use 'said' or an action beat instead.

rules.name: Filter words
rules.desc: Perception filters: felt, saw, heard, noticed, realized, wondered, seemed.
rules.why: Filtering through a character's senses distances the reader (show, don't tell).
rules.fix: Describe the thing perceived directly.
ex: She saw the rain hitting the window.

rules.name: Stock gestures
rules.desc: Overused body language: nodded, shrugged, sighed, grinned, rolled her eyes, raised an eyebrow.
rules.why: Repeated stock beats are the most common line-editing note in fiction.
rules.fix: Cut the beat or replace it with a specific, character-revealing action.
ex: He shrugged. She sighed. He nodded.
He pushed the plate away. She counted the coins twice.

rules.name: Participial openers
rules.desc: Sentences opening with an -ing phrase ('Walking to the door, she…').
rules.why: Overused, they create simultaneous-action errors and a monotonous rhythm.
rules.fix: Vary sentence openings; check the actions can really happen at once.
ex: Opening the door, she crossed the room.
She opened the door and crossed the room.

rules.name: Doubled words
rules.desc: The same word typed twice in a row ('the the').
rules.why: Doubled words are the most common typo that spell-checkers miss.
rules.fix: Delete the duplicate.

rules.name: Spacing errors
rules.desc: Double spaces, space before punctuation, missing space after a comma or full stop.
rules.why: Spacing slips look careless in print and break typesetting.
rules.fix: Fix the spacing at each location.

rules.name: Unbalanced brackets & quotes
rules.desc: Paragraphs where opening and closing brackets or quotation marks don't pair up.
rules.why: An unclosed bracket or quote usually marks a lost edit.
rules.fix: Close or remove the stray mark.

rules.name: Lower-case sentence starts
rules.desc: Sentences that begin with a lower-case letter after a full stop.
rules.why: Usually a missing capital or a stray full stop.
rules.fix: Capitalise the first word or remove the stray full stop.

rules.name: Repeated punctuation
rules.desc: Doubled punctuation such as ,, .. !! ?? or ?!
rules.why: Doubled punctuation is a typo or informal emphasis.
rules.fix: Keep a single mark (use … for an ellipsis).

rules.name: Spelling
rules.desc: Lower-case words not found in the English dictionary on this machine, after allowing for common endings and prefixes.
rules.why: Misspellings are the first thing editors notice and the cheapest thing to fix.
rules.fix: Correct the word, or add genuine technical terms to the custom word list.

ignore_repeated.label: Ignore unknown words used at least this often

rules.name: Heading capitalization
rules.desc: Headings mixing Title Case and Sentence case.
rules.why: House styles pick one heading case and apply it everywhere.
rules.fix: Convert the minority headings to the dominant case.
ex: Data Collection Methods · Results and discussion
Data collection methods · Results and discussion

rules.name: Heading punctuation
rules.desc: Headings ending in a full stop or colon when others don't.
rules.why: Headings normally take no terminal punctuation.
rules.fix: Remove the trailing punctuation.

rules.name: Ellipsis style
rules.why: Use one ellipsis form throughout.
rules.fix: Convert to the dominant form.

rules.name: Dashes
rules.desc: Spaced hyphens or double hyphens used as dashes, and mixed em-dash spacing.
rules.why: A hyphen joins words; dashes (– —) separate clauses and ranges.
rules.fix: Use an en dash (–) for ranges and an em dash (—) for breaks, spaced consistently.

rules.name: Serial comma consistency
rules.desc: Lists of three written both with and without the serial (Oxford) comma.
rules.why: Chicago and APA require it, AP and many UK styles omit it; either way it must be consistent.
rules.fix: Pick one convention and apply it to every list.
ex: red, green, and blue … cats, dogs and birds
red, green, and blue … cats, dogs, and birds

rules.name: Shouting capitals
rules.desc: Ordinary words written in ALL CAPITALS inside sentences.
rules.why: Capitals for emphasis read as shouting; use italics if emphasis is needed.
rules.fix: Write the word normally (italicise if necessary).

rules.name: Missing end punctuation
rules.desc: Paragraphs that stop without a full stop, question mark or other closing mark.
rules.why: A paragraph without terminal punctuation is usually cut off mid-edit.
rules.fix: Finish the sentence and add the full stop.
ex: The groups were then compared on
The groups were then compared on recall.

rules.name: Date format consistency
rules.desc: Mixing date styles (March 5, 2024 / 5 March 2024 / 2024-03-05 / 03/05/2024).
rules.why: One date style throughout; numeric dates are ambiguous between US and UK readers.
rules.fix: Use one written-out style.

rules.name: Time format consistency
rules.desc: Mixing time styles (3 pm / 3 p.m. / 3PM / 15:00).
rules.why: Pick one time convention.
rules.fix: Convert to the dominant style.
ex: at 3 p.m. … at 3:30 p.m. … at 4 p.m.

rules.name: Broken hyphenation
rules.desc: Words split by a line-break hyphen that survived copying ('exam- ple', 'algo-rithm').
rules.why: Leftover line-break hyphens are the classic sign of text pasted from a PDF.
rules.fix: Join the word.

rules.name: Commonly confused words
rules.desc: then/than, its/it's, your/you're, their/there, lose/loose, affect/effect, principal/principle, could of…
rules.why: These slips survive spell-check because each word is spelled correctly.
rules.fix: Use the word suggested.
ex: The nap had more affect then caffeine.
The nap had more effect than caffeine.

rules.name: A / an
rules.desc: 'a' before a vowel sound or 'an' before a consonant sound (a apple, an university, a hour).
rules.why: Article choice follows pronunciation, not spelling.
rules.fix: Use the article suggested.
ex: a hour, an university, a EEG
an hour, a university, an EEG

rules.name: Verb agreement & forms
rules.desc: Agreement slips (they was, the results shows, there is many) and wrong participles (has went, had ran).
rules.why: Agreement errors are among the most distracting grammar mistakes for reviewers.
rules.fix: Use the corrected verb form.
ex: The results shows that they was right.
The results show that they were right.

rules.name: Double negatives
rules.desc: Two negatives cancelling out (did not find no, can't hardly).
rules.why: Double negatives are non-standard and ambiguous in formal English.
rules.fix: Keep one negative.
ex: We did not find no effect.

rules.name: Latin abbreviations
rules.desc: Malformed e.g., i.e., et al., etc. (eg, ie., et. al, etc without full stop) and 'such as … etc.'.
rules.why: Style guides fix exact forms; 'et. al' is the most common citation typo.
rules.fix: Use e.g., i.e., et al., etc.

rules.name: Split infinitives
rules.desc: An adverb between 'to' and its verb (to boldly go).
rules.why: Grammatical, but some conservative house styles still avoid it.
rules.fix: Move the adverb if it reads better; otherwise leave it.

rules.name: Sentence-final prepositions
rules.desc: Sentences ending in a preposition (… to work with.).
rules.why: Not an error in modern English; a few formal house styles still dislike it.
rules.fix: Rephrase only if it sounds awkward.
ex: the method with which we worked.

rules.name: Lower-case 'i'
rules.desc: The pronoun I written as 'i'.
rules.why: An unmistakable typo that undermines credibility.
rules.fix: Capitalise 'I'.

rules.name: Comparatives & less / fewer
rules.desc: Double comparatives (more better), comparing absolutes (most unique, more optimal), less with countable nouns.
rules.why: Absolute adjectives can't be graded; 'fewer' goes with things you can count.
rules.fix: Use the corrected form.
ex: a more optimal, more better approach with less participants
a better approach with fewer participants

rules.name: Apostrophe errors
rules.desc: Apostrophes in plurals (1990's, three PhD's) and 'lets' for 'let's'.
rules.why: Plurals take no apostrophe in every major style guide.
rules.fix: Remove the apostrophe from plurals; write let's for 'let us'.

rules.name: Comma after introductory word
rules.desc: Sentences opening with However, Therefore, For example, In addition… without a comma.
rules.why: A sentence-initial 'However' without a comma means 'in whatever way'.
rules.fix: Add a comma after the introductory word or phrase.

rules.name: Restrictive 'which'
rules.desc: 'which' introducing a clause without a preceding comma (US style uses 'that').
rules.why: Chicago and APA (US) use 'that' for restrictive clauses and ', which' for non-restrictive ones.
rules.fix: Use 'that', or add a comma if the clause is extra information.

rules.name: Comma splices
rules.desc: Two independent clauses joined by a comma and a conjunctive adverb (…, therefore we…).
rules.why: However, therefore and thus are adverbs, not conjunctions; they need a semicolon or full stop before them.
rules.fix: Use a semicolon: '…; therefore, we…'.

rules.name: Hyphen after -ly adverb
rules.desc: Compound modifiers like 'highly-cited' or 'newly-formed'.
rules.why: Every major style guide: no hyphen after an -ly adverb.
rules.fix: Drop the hyphen: 'highly cited'.

rules.name: Sentence fragments
rules.desc: Short sentences that are only a subordinate clause ('Because the data were missing.' 'Which is why.').
rules.why: A dependent clause cannot stand alone in formal writing.
rules.fix: Join the fragment to the sentence before or after it.
ex: We excluded two sessions because the data were missing.

rules.name: Abrupt topic shifts
rules.desc: Consecutive paragraphs in one section that share almost no key words and have no linking word.
rules.why: Readers follow an argument through repeated terms and signposts; an unlinked jump reads as a gap in reasoning.
rules.fix: Open the paragraph with a sentence that ties back to the previous point.
ex: ¶ on sampling → ¶ on budget cuts, no link
¶ on sampling → 'This sample size also shaped the budget…'

rules.name: Disconnected sentences
rules.desc: Consecutive sentences sharing no key word and no linking word (pronoun, demonstrative or transition).
rules.why: Old-before-new ordering (Williams; Gopen & Swan) is what makes prose feel like it flows.
rules.fix: Begin each sentence with something the reader already knows, end with what is new.
ex: Naps help recall. Coffee prices rose in 2020.
Naps help recall. That benefit shrank when participants drank coffee.

rules.name: Missing topic sentences
rules.desc: Long paragraphs (4+ sentences) whose first sentence shares little vocabulary with the rest.
rules.why: A topic sentence tells the reader what the paragraph will prove; skimmers read only first sentences.
rules.fix: Start the paragraph with its main point.
ex: Paragraph opens with a side detail; its point appears in sentence 5.
Paragraph opens with its point; details follow.

rules.name: Circling back
rules.desc: Paragraphs that cover the same ground as an earlier, non-adjacent paragraph.
rules.why: Returning to a point without saying why suggests the structure needs reorganising.
rules.fix: Merge the paragraphs, or state what is new this time.
ex: Explain it once (¶ 3) and refer back: 'As noted, slow-wave sleep…'

rules.name: Interest lulls
rules.desc: Stretches of consecutive paragraphs in the bottom quarter of the document's interest curve.
rules.why: Long flat stretches (no new ideas, little detail, uniform sentences) are where readers stop.
rules.fix: Add an example, a figure, a question or a change of pace.
ex: Six paragraphs of uniform background with no example or number.
Break the stretch with a case, a figure or a question.

rules.name: Citation density
rules.desc: In-text citations ([12], (Smith, 2020), Smith et al. (2020)) per 1,000 words of body text.
rules.why: Scholarly work is expected to situate itself in prior work; sparse citation suggests unsupported claims.
rules.fix: Cite sources for background statements, methods borrowed from others, and comparisons.
ex: Prior studies found mixed results (Lahl et al., 2008; Tucker et al., 2006).

rules.name: Citation-reference match
rules.desc: Citations with no matching reference entry, and reference entries never cited in the text.
rules.why: Every in-text citation must resolve to a reference and every reference must be cited (APA, IEEE, Chicago, Harvard all require this).
rules.fix: Add the missing reference entries and remove or cite the orphaned ones.
ex: Text cites [7]; the list stops at [6].
Every [n] in the text has an entry, every entry is cited.

rules.name: Unsupported claims
rules.desc: Sentences such as 'studies show', 'it is well known', 'experts agree' with no citation in the same or next sentence.
rules.why: Appeals to unnamed authority are the classic reviewer complaint: which studies, which experts?
rules.fix: Add the citation or soften the claim to what you can show.

rules.name: Reference recency
rules.desc: Share of reference entries published more than the age limit before the review year.
rules.why: A literature review dominated by old sources suggests the author has missed recent work.
rules.fix: Add recent sources, or justify reliance on classic work.
ex: A mix of classic work and the last 5–10 years.

rules.name: Reference completeness
rules.desc: Reference entries missing a year, duplicated, or (optionally) missing a DOI/URL.
rules.why: Incomplete references can't be traced; duplicates inflate the list.
rules.fix: Complete each flagged entry and merge duplicates.
ex: Walker, M. Sleep and memory. Unpublished.
Walker, M. P. (2017). Why we sleep. Scribner.

rules.name: Long inline quotations
rules.desc: Quoted passages over the word limit run inline in a paragraph.
rules.why: APA and Chicago require long quotations to be set as block quotes (APA: 40+ words).
rules.fix: Set the quotation as an indented block quote, or paraphrase it.
ex: A 60-word quotation run into the paragraph.
A 60-word quotation set as an indented block.

rules.name: Citation clusters
rules.desc: Single citations listing more than the limit of sources ([3-15], (A; B; C; D; E; F)).
rules.why: Long citation strings hide which source supports what; reviewers call this 'lazy citing'.
rules.fix: Cite the 2-3 most relevant sources, or say what each contributes.
ex: Naps help recall [2] and procedural learning [5].

rules.name: Statistical reporting
rules.desc: p = .000, p values above 1, mixed leading-zero style, means without SD, 'significant' with no statistic.
rules.why: APA 7 §6.36-6.46: report exact p (p < .001 at minimum), dispersion with means, and the test behind each claim.
rules.fix: Fix each flagged value; report test statistic, df, p and effect size together.
ex: p = .000; M = 31.2; the difference was significant.

rules.name: False precision
rules.desc: Numbers with 4 or more decimal places, percentages with 3 or more.
rules.why: Precision beyond what the measurement supports misleads readers.
rules.fix: Round to meaningful precision (usually 2 significant decimals).

rules.name: Weak sources
rules.desc: Reference entries pointing to Wikipedia, blogs, forums, chatbots or personal communications.
rules.why: Tertiary and unvetted sources are not acceptable evidence in scholarly work; APA keeps personal communications out of the list.
rules.fix: Replace with the primary or peer-reviewed source.
ex: Diekelmann, S., & Born, J. (2010). The memory function of sleep. Nat Rev Neurosci.

rules.name: Reference list order
rules.desc: Author-year lists not in alphabetical order; numbered lists not sequential or not in order of first citation.
rules.why: APA/Harvard sort alphabetically; IEEE/Vancouver number in order of first citation.
rules.fix: Re-sort or renumber the reference list.

numbered_by_first_citation.label: Numbered refs must follow first-citation order

rules.name: Overclaiming
rules.desc: Absolute claims: proves, conclusively, undeniably, always, never, everyone knows.
rules.why: Empirical work supports, suggests or demonstrates; it rarely proves.
rules.fix: Calibrate the claim to the evidence.
ex: This proves naps always improve memory.
These results suggest naps can improve recall.

rules.name: Secondary citations
rules.desc: 'as cited in' citations of sources the author did not read.
rules.why: APA allows secondary citation sparingly; heavy use suggests the primary literature wasn't consulted.
rules.fix: Read and cite the original source.

rules.name: Quotations without a source
rules.desc: Direct quotations of 8+ words with no citation in the same or next sentence.
rules.why: Every direct quotation needs a source (and page number in APA/MLA).
rules.fix: Add the citation with page number.
ex: As one researcher put it, “sleep is the price we pay for plasticity.”
As Tononi and Cirelli (2006, p. 52) put it, “sleep is…”

rules.name: Acronyms
rules.desc: Acronyms never defined, used before their definition, or defined more than once.
rules.why: Every style guide requires spelling out an abbreviation at first use.
rules.fix: Define at first use: 'convolutional neural network (CNN)'. Add well-known ones to the allowed list.

rules.name: US / UK spelling mix
rules.desc: Words spelled the American way and the British way in the same document (color / colour, analyze / analyse).
rules.why: Publishers require one spelling convention throughout.
rules.fix: Pick one convention and convert the minority forms.

rules.name: Compound word variants
rules.desc: The same compound written different ways ('dataset', 'data set', 'data-set').
rules.why: Inconsistent compounds look like two different terms to the reader and to search.
rules.fix: Choose one form for each term and use it everywhere.

rules.name: Number & unit style
rules.desc: Mixing % and 'percent', 10000 and 10,000, '5 kg' and '5kg', and sentences that start with a numeral.
rules.why: APA and Chicago both require a consistent number style and spelling out numbers that start a sentence.
rules.fix: Choose one style for each and fix the minority; rewrite sentences that start with a digit.

rules.name: Figure & table references
rules.desc: Figures and tables referenced but never captioned, captioned but never referenced, or numbered with gaps.
rules.why: Every figure and table must be cited in the text, in order (APA 7 §7.4, IEEE).
rules.fix: Add the missing caption or in-text reference and renumber in order.
ex: Text cites Figure 3; only Figures 1–2 exist.
Every figure cited, every cited figure captioned, numbered in order.

rules.name: Quote mark style
rules.desc: Straight quotes (" ') mixed with curly quotes (“ ” ’).
rules.why: Mixed quote styles are a typesetting tell of pasted text.
rules.fix: Convert all quotation marks and apostrophes to one style.

rules.name: Inconsistent capitalization
rules.desc: The same word capitalized mid-sentence in some places and not others (Internet / internet, Chapter / chapter).
rules.why: Capitalization signals a proper noun; switching makes the reader wonder if two things are meant.
rules.fix: Decide whether the term is a proper noun and apply it everywhere.

rules.name: Label abbreviations
rules.desc: Mixing Fig. / Figure, Eq. / Equation, Sec. / Section, Ch. / Chapter in the text.
rules.why: Pick the full or abbreviated label and use it every time.
rules.fix: Use one form of each label.

rules.name: Tense in Methods & Results
rules.desc: Share of present-tense verbs in the Methods and Results sections.
rules.why: APA 7 §4.12: use past tense for what was done and found.
rules.fix: Put procedures and findings in the past tense.
ex: Participants are assigned and the nap group sleeps.
Participants were assigned and the nap group slept.

rules.name: I / we mixing
rules.desc: Author voice switching between 'I' and 'we'.
rules.why: Single authors use 'I' (APA 7) or 'we' consistently; mixing looks like merged drafts.
rules.fix: Use one voice throughout.

rules.name: Small numbers: words vs digits
rules.desc: Numbers one to nine written as words in some places and digits in others.
rules.why: APA and Chicago spell out zero to nine (except with units); be consistent either way.
rules.fix: Use the dominant style for numbers under 10.

rules.name: Name variants
rules.desc: Proper names that differ by one letter (Catherine / Katherine, Jon / John) used multiple times.
rules.why: Inconsistent names are a top continuity error in books and a citation error in papers.
rules.fix: Confirm the correct spelling and fix the others.

rules.name: Reference format consistency
rules.desc: Reference entries formatting the year differently ((2010) vs , 2010.).
rules.why: A single citation style must be applied to every entry.
rules.fix: Reformat the minority entries to the dominant style.

rules.name: Placeholders & draft marks
rules.desc: TODO, TBD, FIXME, XXX, [citation needed], 'Figure ??', 'Error! Reference source not found', lorem ipsum.
rules.why: Placeholders mean the manuscript is not finished. Editors desk-reject on sight.
rules.fix: Resolve every placeholder before submission.
ex: TODO: add the Smith review here. [citation needed]

rules.name: Repeated text
rules.desc: Identical sentences (10+ words) and near-identical paragraphs appearing more than once.
rules.why: Duplicated text is usually a copy-paste accident, and plagiarism checkers flag it as self-overlap.
rules.fix: Delete the repetition or rewrite one instance.
ex: The same 30-word sentence in the introduction and discussion.
Said once; the discussion refers back to it.

rules.name: Stub sections
rules.desc: Sections with fewer than the minimum words of their own and no subsections.
rules.why: A heading with almost nothing under it is an unfinished section.
rules.fix: Write the section out or merge it into its neighbour.
ex: 2.2 Materials: a full description of the 40 pairs and how they were chosen.

rules.name: Declarations & statements
rules.desc: End-matter statements the venue expects: keywords, data availability, competing interests, funding.
rules.why: Most journals (COPE, ICMJE, Springer Nature, Elsevier) now require these statements.
rules.fix: Add each missing statement, even if it only says 'none'.
ex: Funding: none. Data availability: OSF, doi:10.17605/…

rules.name: Open tracked changes & comments
rules.desc: Unaccepted tracked changes and reviewer comments still embedded in a Word or OpenDocument file.
rules.why: Open revisions leak editing history and confuse typesetters.
rules.fix: Accept or reject all changes and delete comments before submitting.
ex: 12 tracked changes and 4 comments still open

rules.name: Encoding damage
rules.desc: Replacement characters (�), mojibake (â€™, Ã©) and control characters.
rules.why: Broken encoding means text was converted badly and will print as garbage.
rules.fix: Re-export the file as UTF-8 and fix the damaged characters.

rules.name: Empty brackets
rules.desc: Empty or punctuation-only brackets: (), [], [ , ].
rules.why: Usually a deleted citation or a field that never filled in.
rules.fix: Fill in or delete.

rules.name: Export & copy-paste artifacts
rules.desc: 'Page 3 of 10', 'Downloaded from', 'Click here', Word comment markers [AB1], 'Formatted:', 'All rights reserved' in the body.
rules.why: Artifacts show the text was pasted from another document without cleaning.
rules.fix: Delete the artifact.
ex: Downloaded from journals.example.org on 3 May … Page 4 of 12

rules.name: AI-assistant leftovers
rules.desc: Phrases chatbots leave in pasted text: 'As an AI language model', 'I hope this helps', 'Certainly! Here is', 'Regenerate response'.
rules.why: Publishers require disclosure of AI use; leftover chatbot text is grounds for desk rejection.
rules.fix: Remove the text and disclose AI assistance as your venue requires.
ex: Certainly! Here is a revised version of your paragraph:
(removed; AI use disclosed in the methods if required)

rules.name: Personal data
rules.desc: Email addresses, phone numbers and ID-like numbers in the text.
rules.why: Personal data in a manuscript is a privacy risk and breaks anonymous review.
rules.fix: Remove or move to the title page if required.

rules.name: Links
rules.desc: Bare URLs in sentences, insecure http:// links, URL shorteners, local paths (localhost, C:\, file://).
rules.why: Links belong in citations; shorteners and local paths break for every other reader.
rules.fix: Cite the source properly; use the full https address.
ex: see the dataset (Doe, 2024) in the references

rules.name: Double-blind anonymity
rules.desc: Self-identifying phrases: 'our previous work', 'we previously showed', 'our lab', acknowledgements present.
rules.why: Double-blind venues reject submissions that reveal the authors.
rules.fix: Refer to your own work in the third person; move acknowledgements to the title page.
ex: As we showed in our previous work (Doe, 2022)…

rules.name: Draft language
rules.desc: DRAFT, 'do not cite', 'to be completed', 'fix this', 'check this', 'needs more work'.
rules.why: Notes to self left in the text signal an unfinished manuscript.
rules.fix: Resolve and delete each note.
ex: DRAFT – check this – to be completed

rules.name: Duplicate headings
rules.desc: The same heading text used for two sections at the same level.
rules.why: Duplicate headings break navigation and usually mean a pasted section.
rules.fix: Merge the sections or give them distinct headings.

rules.name: Appendix references
rules.desc: Appendices referenced but missing, or present but never referenced.
rules.why: Each appendix must be cited in the text, and cited appendices must exist.
rules.fix: Add the appendix or the reference to it.
ex: See Appendix C (no Appendix C exists).

paper.name: Research paper
paper.blurb: Journal or conference article. IMRaD structure, citations, declarations.

chapter.name: Book chapter
chapter.blurb: Non-fiction or academic chapter. Readability and flow weigh more; citations lighter.

book.name: Full book
book.blurb: Whole non-fiction manuscript. Chapter balance, consistency and readability lead.

fiction.name: Fiction
fiction.blurb: Novel, story or narrative chapter. Prose style matters most; no citations or IMRaD.

general.name: General document
general.blurb: Reports, essays, proposals, documentation. Balanced defaults.
